title: In the Big Stablecoin Fight, Will Crypto Firms, Fintechs or Banks Win?
abstract:
PART 1 — ABSTRACT

This conversation centers on the accelerating competition to build the dominant stablecoin and real-world asset (RWA) blockchain infrastructure, examining whether crypto-native firms, fintechs, or traditional banks will ultimately control the space. It probes why specialized stablecoin blockchains are proliferating, highlighting how the clash between crypto ideals—like decentralization and censorship-resistance—and the practical, centralized demands of financial institutions shapes infrastructure design and adoption. The discussion argues that regulatory forces and entrenched scale, rather than technological innovation, will be the key determinants, potentially limiting disruptive potential and favoring incumbent banks. Still, questions persist about how much decentralization will remain, whether new entrants can overcome distribution moats, and if consumer or institutional benefits will materialize amid competition, technical tradeoffs, and unresolved risks around security and reversibility.

PART 2 — KEY IDEAS

- The real-world requirements for payments (e.g. reversibility, dispute resolution, predictable fees) favor purpose-built blockchains over public general-purpose chains like Ethereum.
- Major payment processors like Stripe have an advantage through existing merchant networks and their ability to bridge traditional finance and blockchain activity at scale.
- Most current “upstart” players may be temporary leaders; large global banks and payment companies, when they enter, could overwhelm them due to superior distribution, scale, and regulatory positioning.
- Liquidity and yield, not “sticky” network effects, drive financial markets, making it difficult for new entrants to build defensible advantages without massive capital or integration.
- The core value of stablecoins lies in breaking the current banking paradigm, potentially unbundling banking functions and delivering better financial products for consumers—regardless of which platform prevails.
- There is tension between decentralization and the practical need for asset controls (e.g., reversibility if an issuer or smart contract is compromised), and fully decentralized blockchains are not yet ready for prime-time real-world asset issuance.
- Existing public blockchains, especially Ethereum, lack mature risk management tools compared to what’s standard in traditional finance, making them vulnerable to catastrophic scenarios not yet contemplated by on-chain governance.
- Consortium or permissioned models (such as Avalanche subnets or Stellar) may offer a better institutional fit by balancing credible neutrality with control and regulatory compliance.
- The outcome is unlikely to be a single winner; instead, market structure is expected to fragment, with different blockchains and models serving different user segments and geographic markets (e.g., Tether in global south, USDC in the US).
- Regulation is emerging as the ultimate “kingmaker;” however, rapid technological and institutional evolution means the landscape could change over the next five to ten years, and consumer benefit could accrue even if no new “Facebook of stablecoins” emerges.
